…especially evident in research that conflates technical ‘ capabilities ’ with lived, emergent action potentials, overlooking the central afford-ance principle that opportunities for action only exist in the relational ‘ in-between ’ of the learner and the environment (Gibson, 1979; van Lier, 2004).
Perceptibility is fundamental because unperceived affordances are effectively non-affordances in practice (Gibson, 1979; van Lier, 2004; Wei et al., 2022; Xie & Rice, 2021).
Valence is frequently present but remains implicit rather than systematically analyzed (Gibson, 1979; Norman, 1988; Gaver, 1991).

The ecological and complexity-informed tradition has long emphasized that affordances cannot be reduced to stable functionalities or universal advantages but must always be considered in action and ecologically based (Gibson, 1979; Larsen-Freeman & Cameron, 2008; van Lier, 2004).

These findings are consistent with ecological and complexity-informed perspectives emphasizing how learning opportunities become meaningful through learners ’ evolving engagement (Gibson, 1979; Larsen-Freeman & Cameron, 2008; van Lier, 2004).
Nearly all major theories explicitly address perceptibility, though the level of detail and centrality varies (Gibson, 1979; Kirschner, 2002; Norman, 1988; van Lier, 2004).

Affordance uptake is therefore idiographic, situated, and emergent, extending ecological and complexity-informed approaches in applied linguistics (Gibson, 1979; Larsen-Freeman & Cameron, 2008; van Lier, 2004).
The concept of affordance originates from ecological psychology (Gibson, 1979), referring to the action possibilities that the environment ‘ offers ’ or provides to an agent.

…van Lier recasts language learnin g not as the incremental processing of linguistic input, nor as movement along a single developmental continuum, but as the ongoing perception and enactment of affordances embedded in richly complex environments (Chemero, 2009; Gibson, 1979; van Lier, 2004).
The concept of affordances, introduced by Gibson, is foundational to the ecological approach to perception and action (Gibson, 1979).

This article’s theoretical stance explicitly returns to the Gibsonian concept: affordances are emergent, relational possibilities for action, realized only through aligning learner intentions, abilities, and contextual resources (Chemero, 2003; Gibson, 1979; Withagen et al., 2012).

Without systematic attention to perceptibility, learners and educational practitioners risk overestimating the impact of designed features or environments by assuming that all learners notice and can engage with available opportunities (Gibson, 1979; Reinders & White, 2016).
Affordance theory, articulated within ecological psychology, offers a powerful way to address these needs (Chemero, 2009; Gibson, 1979).

While ecological psychology explains how opportunities for action are always relational and situated (Chemero, 2009; Gibson, 1979), rhizomatic learning further illuminates how learning pathways multiply and evolve through flexible, networked engagement (Lian & Pineda, 2014; Mackness et al., 2016).
